concepts.title: Every French noun has a gender
concepts.shortRule: Every noun is masculine (le) or feminine (la) — the article is part of the word.
concepts.explanation: French sorts all nouns into two grammatical classes, masculine and feminine. This is a property of the word itself, not of the thing it names, so the reliable way to learn a noun is to learn it together with its article: 'le chat', 'la pomme'. The good news: a noun's ENDING often signals its gender, and the upcoming lessons teach only the ending patterns that a 36,940-noun analysis shows to be genuinely dependable.

examples.note: before a vowel sound the article shortens to l', hiding the gender — eau is feminine

exceptions: Before a vowel sound, both le and la become l', so the article stops showing the gender. For those nouns, remember them with un/une instead: une eau minérale.

concepts.title: Endings that say « feminine »
concepts.shortRule: Nouns ending in -tion, -ance, -ence, -ité or -ie are almost always feminine.
concepts.explanation: You do not have to memorize every noun's gender one by one — the ending often decides it. In an analysis of 36,940 French nouns, words ending in -tion are feminine 99.5% of the time, -ance 98.9%, -ence 98.3%, -ité 97.8%, and -ie 96.3%. When you meet a new noun with one of these endings, say « la » with confidence.
exceptions: "Almost always" is not "always": a rare exception exists for each ending — but with reliability this high, guessing feminine is the right habit.

concepts.title: Endings that say « masculine »
concepts.shortRule: Nouns ending in -ment, -age, -eau or -ier are usually masculine.
concepts.explanation: The masculine side has strong ending patterns too, from the same 36,940-noun analysis: -ment is masculine 99.8% of the time, -age 98.5%, -eau 96.7%, and -ier 97.1%. Meet a new noun with one of these endings and « le » is very likely right.
exceptions: l'eau (water) is feminine — the most famous exception to -eau.
l'image (the picture) and la page are feminine -age words: -age is "usually", not "always".

concepts.title: Two endings that need care
concepts.shortRule: -on is usually masculine — but -ion and -son words inside it are feminine. -eur is usually masculine — with famous feminine exceptions.
concepts.explanation: Two common endings hide sub-patterns. Nouns in -on are masculine 96.7% of the time ONCE you set aside the -ion family (feminine: la question) and the -son family (feminine: la maison, la raison). And -eur nouns are masculine 92.5% of the time, but several very frequent ones are feminine. Learn the sub-families, not just the last two letters.
exceptions: Frequent feminine -eur nouns: la peur (fear), l'erreur (the mistake), la couleur (the color), la fleur (the flower).
The -son sub-family: la maison, la raison, la saison, la chanson — feminine.
concepts.memoryHint: See -ion or -son? Think la. Other -on? Think le.

concepts.title: Être and avoir — the two anchor verbs
concepts.shortRule: je suis / tu es / il est · j'ai / tu as / il a — learn these six forms cold.
concepts.explanation: The two most-used verbs in French are also the most irregular, so their présent forms are learned as words, not from a pattern: être (to be) — je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont; avoir (to have) — j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. They repay the effort twice: they carry everyday sentences now, and later they build the past tense for every other verb.

examples.en: You are right (literally: you have reason).

exceptions: French uses avoir where English uses be in fixed phrases: avoir faim (to be hungry), avoir raison (to be right), avoir 20 ans (to be 20 years old).
Before a vowel, je shortens: j'ai, never 'je ai'.
concepts.memoryHint: sont = they are, ont = they have — the s belongs to être.

concepts.title: -er verbs: six spellings, three sounds
concepts.shortRule: parle, parles and parlent are all pronounced the same — endings change on paper more than in speech.
concepts.explanation: Regular -er verbs (the largest verb family) all conjugate like parler: je parle, tu parles, il/elle parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent. In speech those six forms collapse to three sounds — parle/parles/parlent all sound like 'parl' (Lexique 4 phonology: /paʁl/), parlons has its own sound, and parlez sounds exactly like the infinitive parler (/paʁle/). So when you speak, the pronoun does most of the work; the written endings matter most when you type or write.

examples.note: vous: stem + ez — sounds like the infinitive

exceptions: Verbs in -ger keep the e before -ons to protect the soft g: nous mangeons, never 'mangons'.
Aller looks like an -er verb but is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il va.
concepts.memoryHint: If the subject is je/tu/il/ils, an -er verb usually SOUNDS like its bare stem.

concepts.title: Talking about the future with aller
concepts.shortRule: aller (présent) + infinitive = going to: Je vais manger — I am going to eat.
concepts.explanation: French has a simple future you can use from day one: conjugate aller in the présent and follow it with any infinitive, exactly like English 'going to'. Je vais parler (I'm going to speak), tu vas manger, nous allons habiter à Lyon. You only ever conjugate aller — the second verb stays in the dictionary form — so six memorized forms of aller unlock future statements with every verb you know.

examples.fr: Nous allons parler avec le patron.
examples.en: We are going to talk with the boss.
They are going to take a trip.

exceptions: Aller alone also means physically going somewhere: Je vais au bureau — I am going to the office. Context tells you which reading is meant.
concepts.memoryHint: aller + infinitive works just like English 'going to + verb'.

concepts.title: The past with avoir + participle
concepts.shortRule: avoir (présent) + past participle = did / have done: J'ai mangé — I ate.
concepts.explanation: The everyday French past tense is built from two pieces you already have: the présent of avoir plus the verb's past participle. For -er verbs the participle just swaps -er for -é (parler → parlé, manger → mangé), so J'ai parlé = I spoke, Tu as mangé = you ate, Nous avons habité = we lived. Some verbs have participles to memorize — être → été, avoir → eu, faire → fait — but the frame never changes.
exceptions: A small set of movement/change verbs (aller among them) build this tense with être instead of avoir: Je suis allé — I went. That set is taught as its own list later.
concepts.memoryHint: -er verb? Its participle is the infinitive sound spelled -é.
